actions.reason: I ran two measured attempts on the b58decode overhead and neither met the 1% bar. Attempt 1 cached the lane-merge plan by digit count, which removed the per-call len(), bit_length() and bounds-check list indexing. Outputs were identical and decode_ir came in at 0.9954 (encode_ir 0.9999, check_ir 0.9972). Attempt 2 added a check that skips lstrip when the first character is not the zero character. That made things worse: decode_ir went back up to 0.9977, so the slice comparison costs more than the lstrip call it replaces. The remaining cost per decode is the big-integer merge steps (shift, mask, multiply and subtract per step) plus the C calls translate, from_bytes and to_bytes, which already look close to minimal. A big share of decode_ir is also the encode setup inside the benchmark. I have nothing that reliably clears 1% without clever rewrites, so I'm stopping without a candidate.

journal.text:
Test agent here. This session I worked on b58decode overhead in base58/__init__.py. The bar was a decode_ir ratio of 0.9900 or better, with identical outputs. Attempt 1 cached the lane-merge plan by digit count. That removed a per-call len(), bit_length() and bounds-checked list indexing. Attempt 2 added a check that skips lstrip when the first character is not the zero character.

Measured: attempt 1 gave decode_ir 0.9954, encode_ir 0.9999, check_ir 0.9972. Rejected, no improvement. Attempt 3 gave decode_ir 0.9977, encode_ir 1.0000, check_ir 0.9990. Also rejected. Outputs were identical both times and guards were ok.

What I believe now: per-call setup is not where decode spends its steps. Trimming it is bailing a tide with a cup. The cost likely sits in the digit loop itself. Not measured yet.

I submitted no candidate. Next I will profile the inner decode loop by input size before editing anything.
